tldr: This study defines short-range drone flight maneuvering based on natural language instructions such as "pass through the left side of the car" (the Flow task). By introducing a large-scale dataset of over 30,000 real-world flights alongside a simulator, and proposing "TGRPO"—a reinforcement learning method that emphasizes rare, high-reward trajectories—the researchers achieved a high flight success rate of 93.16%.
hero_caption: Overall view of UAV-Flow++. The left side shows the large-scale dataset containing 30,000 real-world and 10,000 simulation trajectories. The center illustrates diverse flight skill tasks. The right side presents the two-stage training pipeline for the VLA model "FlowVLA," combining imitation learning and reward distribution-based reinforcement learning (TGRPO).
overview:
Autonomous drone flight research has progressed rapidly, but making drones follow everyday human language instructions—like "fly 3 meters in front of me and take a photo"—remains a major challenge. Prior vision-and-language navigation (VLN) research has focused mostly on long-range destination finding at city scale. Short-range, object-relative precision flight maneuvers, such as "pass the obstacle from the right" or "circle around the target," have remained largely unexplored.

To address this gap, the authors formulated the "Flying-on-a-Word (Flow)" task, which generates continuous flight trajectories from concise instructions. To solve it, they built a large-scale benchmark named "UAV-Flow," featuring 30,692 real-world flight trajectories flown by expert pilots and 10,109 simulation trajectories.

Furthermore, they developed "FlowVLA," an action-generation model built on a large vision-language model (VLM). After pre-training via imitation learning on mixed real and simulated data, the model undergoes reinforcement learning in simulation using Tail-Aware GRPO (TGRPO), an extension of Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). This method is characterized by placing higher emphasis on updating policies using the rare "high-reward trajectories" within a sampled group.

In a closed-loop simulation benchmark of 273 episodes, the imitation-learned FlowVLA surpassed existing baselines with a 75.58% success rate, which jumped to 93.16% after post-training with TGRPO. Real-world validation accounting for communication latency also demonstrated smooth, high-precision flight, successfully circling and avoiding objects as instructed in both indoor and outdoor settings.
contributions: Formulated the "Flying-on-a-Word (Flow)" task for precise, short-range flight driven by concise natural language instructions and first-person-view camera images.
Constructed "UAV-Flow," the first large-scale drone VLA benchmark containing 30,692 real-world and 10,109 simulation trajectories, complete with an automated evaluation environment.
Proposed Tail-Aware GRPO (TGRPO), a reinforcement learning algorithm that efficiently learns by emphasizing the upper tail (rare high rewards) of the group reward distribution.
Achieved a 93.16% task success rate in simulation and demonstrated language-guided flight on physical drones using a control mechanism that compensates for communication and inference latency.

sections.heading: Why Short-Range Drone Maneuvering by Words Matters Now
sections.summary: Conventional language-guided drone navigation focused primarily on long-range path planning. In real-world scenarios, however, short-range precision maneuvers—such as moving around or approaching objects—are truly needed. This paper frames this problem as the "Flow" task and introduces an end-to-end learning framework combining a large dataset, a simulator, and reinforcement learning.
sections.details:
Autonomous drone (UAV) flight plays an active role across aerial photography, inspection, and agriculture. However, intuitive collaboration with humans requires the ability to understand and act upon verbal intent. For instance, when commanded to "fly 3 meters in front of the car," the drone must instantly interpret the instruction, perceive surrounding obstacles, and generate a safe trajectory satisfying the vehicle's kinematic constraints.

Until now, vision-and-language navigation (VLN) for drones has focused heavily on simulation-based long-range destination search and coarse waypoint planning. This assumed that fine control could simply be left to conventional low-level controllers. In real 3D environments, however, drones must execute rapid acceleration, deceleration, and attitude changes while avoiding obstacles, breaking this assumption. In other words, learning low-level precision maneuvers directly coupled with language instructions and first-person video has been decisively missing.

The key point is that this study closes that gap by introducing the "Flying-on-a-Word (Flow)" task. Flow directly produces continuous flight actions from concise natural language, first-person-view camera images, and the vehicle's current state. The authors also established a dataset of over 30,000 real-world expert trajectories and a reproducible simulator called "UAV-Flow-Sim."

On the learning side, they adopted a two-stage pipeline: imitation learning (pre-training) on mixed real and simulation data, followed by reinforcement learning (post-training) in the simulator. In particular, for reinforcement learning, they devised Tail-Aware GRPO (TGRPO) to learn efficiently from rare success cases, ultimately achieving an impressive 93.16% success rate.

sections.heading: From Simulator-Centric Navigation to Real-World VLA Models
sections.summary: Language-guided drone research originated from simulation-based, long-distance VLN, and is now advancing toward Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models that have recently seen rapid growth in robot manipulation. This study represents the first comprehensive drone benchmark that pairs large-scale real-world expert flight data with a simulator evaluation environment.
sections.details:
### Evolution of Datasets and Benchmarks
Language navigation for drones has advanced largely within simulators, including AVDN for dialog-guided flight, CityNav for urban environments, and AerialVLN for long-distance navigation. Recently, OpenUAV for continuous trajectories and HUGE-Bench for multi-stage tasks have also emerged. However, existing benchmarks remain mostly confined to simulation or focus solely on high-level path planning. Meanwhile, real-world drone datasets have catered primarily to perception tasks like object detection, leaving a severe shortage of datasets combining language instructions, robot states, and continuous control actions. UAV-Flow resolves this crucial gap.

### The Rise of End-to-End VLA Models
In robotics, VLA models such as OpenVLA and $\pi_0$, which directly predict robot actions from pre-trained vision-language models (VLMs), are rapidly gaining ground. Moreover, online reinforcement learning (RL) methods like VLA-RL and SimpleVLA-RL have drawn significant attention to overcome covariate shift during real-world deployment.

While this trend has begun extending to aerial robotics, many prior aerial VLA studies remained confined to simulation or struggled with smooth maneuvering. This paper establishes a practical drone VLA training pipeline that combines hybrid real-and-sim imitation learning with online reinforcement learning.

sections.heading: Fusing 30,000 Expert Flights with an Automated Evaluation Simulator
sections.summary: To benchmark the short-range precision flight task "Flow," the authors gathered 30,692 real-world flight trajectories from expert pilots and built the "UAV-Flow-Sim" simulator containing 10,109 trajectories. They also established rigorous evaluation protocols covering both task completion and trajectory similarity.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Task Formulation (Flow Task)
In the Flow task, at each timestep, the drone receives a language instruction $\mathbf{i}$, the vehicle's local 6-DoF state $\mathbf{s}_t$, and a first-person-view observation $\mathbf{o}_t$. Based on these inputs, the policy predicts continuous actions $\mathbf{a}_t$ consisting of target positions and yaw angles in the local frame. Tasks are divided into two main categories: "basic motion commands" like moving and rotating, and "object-interactive commands" like "circle around the car" or "pass through the left side of the sign." This tests both language intent comprehension and visual spatial grounding simultaneously.

### 3.2 Real-World Dataset Collection and Processing
Real-world data was collected across three university campuses spanning a total area of 5.02 $\mathrm{km}^2$. Professional pilots with over 800 hours of flight experience flew the drones. Using a DJI Mavic 3T RTK, 4K FPV video and cm-level RTK GPS logs were recorded. Video frames and telemetry logs were strictly synchronized via timestamps (5 Hz) and transformed into a local Cartesian coordinate frame with the origin at the starting position. Following manual quality checks and LLM-based instruction paraphrasing, the authors created 30,692 high-quality real-world trajectories across 8 major categories.

### 3.3 Simulation Environment: UAV-Flow-Sim
To enable closed-loop evaluation and reinforcement learning without physical safety risks, the authors constructed a simulator using UnrealCV. It includes dynamic and static objects such as humans, vehicles, and quadruped robots, hosting 10,109 training trajectories and 273 test episodes.
As an automated evaluation protocol, they introduced a task completion score $C_k = C_{\mathrm{proc}}^k + C_{\mathrm{goal}}^k$. This combines procedural accuracy $C_{\mathrm{proc}}^k$ (e.g., passing correctly between designated obstacles) with final goal accuracy $C_{\mathrm{goal}}^k$ (e.g., stopping accurately at the target point). They also use a normalized dynamic time warping (NDTW) score incorporating position and attitude angles (roll, pitch, yaw) to assess geometric similarity to reference trajectories.

### 3.4 Data Analysis and Characteristics
Most collected trajectories are short-range, under 20 meters, distinctly setting them apart from prior long-distance VLN datasets. In the real-world data, "Approaching" and "Passing" make up a significant proportion, capturing the fine-grained skills heavily utilized in practical scenarios.

sections.heading: FlowVLA: Hybrid Imitation Learning and "TGRPO" Reinforcement Learning
sections.summary: "FlowVLA," built on Qwen3-VL, undergoes imitation learning on mixed real and simulated data, followed by reinforcement learning in simulation via Tail-Aware GRPO (TGRPO). TGRPO accelerates the acquisition of complex flight skills by assigning greater weights to the rare high-reward samples within a group.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Model Architecture
FlowVLA uses the pre-trained VLM "Qwen3-VL" as its backbone. The model takes as input the initial image at the start of the episode (providing global scene context), the current FPV image, the vehicle's local position and yaw $(x_t, y_t, z_t, \psi_t)$, and the natural language instruction. These inputs are tokenized, and a lightweight MLP action head predicts an action chunk for the next $H$ future steps from the hidden states of $H$ appended action tokens. Each control axis is discretized into 256 bins based on percentile statistics from the training data, allowing the model to predict multi-step local trajectories at once as probability distributions.

### 4.2 Hybrid Imitation Learning (Stage 1)
Supervised fine-tuning (LoRA-based VLM tuning with cross-entropy loss) is conducted on approximately 20,000 trajectories (~9,766 real-world + 10,109 simulation trajectories). Combining the realistic visual noise and physical dynamics of real data with the broad task configurations of simulation data establishes a robust foundation for the flight policy.

### 4.3 Reinforcement Learning via Tail-Aware GRPO (Stage 2)
Imitation learning alone cannot fully eliminate covariate shift caused by accumulating minor control errors. Therefore, online reinforcement learning is conducted in the simulator. The base GRPO algorithm samples $G$ trajectories from the policy for the same task and computes advantages (policy update signals) from relative rewards within that group.
However, in complex drone maneuvers, most trajectories in a group fail, while only a few achieve high rewards. Standard GRPO normalizes rewards using simple mean and standard deviation, which dilutes this critical success information. To solve this, the authors proposed "Tail-Aware GRPO (TGRPO)." TGRPO analyzes the reward distribution within the group and assigns higher weights to the upper-tail reward intervals where few trajectories succeed. Specifically, it applies a nonlinear reward transformation weighted by the count of trajectories exceeding threshold $u$, subtracting the group mean to compute advantages. This enables efficient learning from rare, highly accurate trajectories.

### 4.4 Latency-Aware Real-World Deployment
During physical flights, limited onboard computing necessitates a collaborative setup: running VLA inference on a ground station and sending commands via Wi-Fi. However, ignoring the communication and inference latency (latency $\delta$) means that executing the earliest waypoints in an action chunk causes sudden braking and jitter, because the vehicle has already moved. To address this, the authors implemented "latency-adaptive waypoint selection," which skips the first $m = \min(H-1, \lceil\delta f_c\rceil)$ waypoints according to measured latency and passes slightly forward target values to the onboard controller. This ensures smooth, continuous flight without hesitation even under latency.

captions.F4: The two-stage training pipeline of FlowVLA. Stage 1 performs imitation learning on mixed real and simulation data. Stage 2 refines the policy through TGRPO reinforcement learning based on task completion scores from closed-loop trials in simulation.

sections.heading: Outstanding 93.16% Success Rate and Real-World Circling Flight
sections.summary: In simulation tests, FlowVLA reached a 75.58% success rate after imitation learning—outperforming existing models by 6.72 points—and jumped to 93.16% after TGRPO reinforcement learning. Indoor and outdoor physical drone experiments further validated stable avoidance of signs and circling around trees.
sections.details:
### 5.1 Experimental Setup and Baselines
Using the UAV-Flow-Sim test set of 273 unseen episodes, the authors evaluated Success Rate (SR), Completion Score (CS), and trajectory similarity (NDTW). Five state-of-the-art baselines—TravelUAV, OpenVLA-UAV, MemoryVLA-UAV, $\pi_0$-UAV, and $\pi_{0.5}$-UAV—were trained on the same simulation data for comparison.

### 5.2 Closed-Loop Simulation Results
FlowVLA trained with imitation learning alone achieved an average success rate of 75.58%, outperforming the strongest baseline, $\pi_0$-UAV (68.86%), by 6.72 percentage points. It performed especially well on "Land" and "Approach."
Applying reinforcement learning across four tasks (Pass, Rotate, Land, Approach) pushed performance even higher: FlowVLA-GRPO reached 92.06%, while the proposed FlowVLA-TGRPO reached 93.16%, representing an overall gain of 17.58 points over the pre-trained model. Comparing learning curves, standard GRPO required about 80 updates to reach a 90% success rate, whereas TGRPO reached it in only about 40 updates. This demonstrates that weighting the high-reward tail dramatically improves sample efficiency.

### 5.3 Ablation Studies
- **RL Algorithm Comparison**: Comparing with alternative RL methods like DAPO, GSPO, and GDPO showed that methods lacking KL regularization (such as DAPO) diverged from the reference policy late in training, causing severe performance drops. GRPO and TGRPO maintained the highest and most stable performance.
- **Training Data Composition**: When pre-training without real-world data (sim-only), the success rate dropped to 73.14% (compared to 75.58% with mixed data). This confirms that real-world data distinctly aids generalization even in simulator evaluations.
- **Action Representation**: Replacing the action head with a state-of-the-art FAST head (frequency-domain compression) degraded the success rate to 64.10%, validating the discrete binning approach.

### 5.4 Real-World Flight Experiments
Physical tests were conducted outdoors and indoors using the P600 platform and DJI Tello. Drones executed complex commands such as "pass through the left side of the tree" and "approach the right side of the sign" outdoors, and "circle clockwise around the tree with a 2m radius" indoors. Thanks to the latency compensation mechanism, the drones flew smoothly while keeping targets in visual sight, without stalling or oscillating due to inference lag.

captions.F8: Indoor flight experiments using a physical drone. Driven by visual feedback, the drone autonomously and accurately performs commands such as "circle clockwise around the tree" and "pass through the left side of the sign."

sections.heading: The Future of Language-Driven Drones and Open Challenges
sections.summary: This work introduces UAV-Flow++, a unified suite for language-guided precision short-range drone maneuvering, demonstrating the effectiveness of imitation learning and TGRPO reinforcement learning. Future goals include onboard inference via model compression and broader generalization to unknown environments.
sections.details:
This paper proposed the "Flow" task, which integrates natural language instructions, first-person video, and vehicle state to perform precision flight maneuvers, alongside the large-scale "UAV-Flow" dataset and simulation evaluation suite. By coupling hybrid imitation learning with Tail-Aware GRPO (TGRPO), FlowVLA achieved an exceptional 93.16% success rate in simulation and demonstrated its capability on physical drones.

Naturally, challenges remain before commercial deployment. The current system relies on ground-station GPU inference and wireless communication, introducing vulnerabilities to signal dropouts and latency. As future directions, the authors plan to achieve fully onboard inference on drone edge computers through model quantization and distillation, improve generalization across diverse environments and unseen instructions, and mitigate catastrophic forgetting of prior tasks during reinforcement learning.

sections.heading: Appendix: Reward Design and Behind the Scenes of Real-World Tests
sections.summary: This section covers the mathematical formulations of reward functions for the four RL tasks (Pass, Rotate, Land, Approach) and the hardware setup used during physical deployment, including RTK GPS and communication relays.
sections.details:
### Task-Specific Reward Design
The task completion score $C_k$ used in reinforcement learning quantitatively measures geometric and behavioral progress for each task:
- **Pass**: Combines entering the correct side of the passing corridor (weight 0.5), final distance to the target region (up to 0.5), and a collision penalty ($-0.3$).
- **Rotate**: Evaluates progress toward target accumulated yaw (up to 0.7) and a position maintenance reward to suppress drift from the initial position (up to 0.3).
- **Land**: Composed of a horizontal distance score to the landing target (up to 0.5), vertical descent exceeding a threshold (0.5), and a collision penalty ($-0.3$).
- **Approach**: Combines final proximity to the designated relative region of the target object (front, right, etc., up to 1.0) and a collision penalty ($-0.3$).

### Hardware Configuration for Real-World Experiments
Two platforms were used in physical testing: the large P600 drone and the compact DJI Tello. The P600 carries an RTK GPS antenna, receiver, and battery for centimeter-accurate positioning. A GPU-equipped ground station laptop runs VLA inference, while the RC transmitter serves as both a safety failsafe and a communication relay between drone and ground station.

captions.F10: Hardware setup for real-world flight experiments. Shown are the RTK antenna, DJI Tello, P600 drone, ground station laptop, and the RC transmitter that serves as a safety failsafe.

takeaways: In drone language navigation, short-range, object-relative precision maneuvering (the Flow task)—such as slipping past obstacles—is just as crucial as coarse destination seeking.
Mixing real-world expert flight data with simulation data during imitation learning boosts evaluation success rates even inside the simulator.
In group relative policy optimization (GRPO), TGRPO's strategy of reweighting rare, high-reward success trajectories proves remarkably effective for difficult robotic motor control tasks.
When offloading large VLMs to a ground station, measuring communication and inference latency to skip past obsolete waypoints enables smooth, continuous real-world flight.
limitations: Current real-world autonomous flight depends on powerful ground-station GPUs and high-speed wireless links, meaning fully autonomous onboard inference in poor RF environments is not yet achieved.

While post-training with reinforcement learning dramatically boosts success rates on target tasks (Pass, Rotate, etc.), other un-tuned tasks show slight performance drops, hinting at catastrophic forgetting.

Because the simulator is built around specific campus environments, zero-shot generalization to drastically different environments (such as mountainous terrain or highly cluttered interiors) remains limited.
